catalog_quote: All words in Slovene that are not clitics have at least one prominent syllable. Prominence is lexically determined, i.e., it is not predictable, so it is a feature of the word which must be learned along with the segmental sequence and the meaning. Prominence is marked in at least two broadly different ways depending on which dialect area a Slovene speaker comes from. Speakers from Ljubljana, the Upper and Lower Carniolan dialects, or the Carinthian dialect may have a pitch-accent (“tonemic”) system. Speakers from other areas generally have a dynamic stress (“stress”) system. In both the tonemic and stress systems, vestiges of a quantity opposition in stressed syllables may still be realized in many speakers’ systems. With the exception of some peripheral dialects, distinctions between long and short stressed syllables occur in the final or only syllable. ... Stress placement, vowel qua…
sweep_summary: Three title-hits for Slovenian. (1) Greenberg 2003 (STUF) — obtained (KU ScholarWorks copy via Wayback; KU blocks this host) and read: word stress is assigned by a morpheme-level lexical accent algorithm (stress on the first rising-accented morpheme, falling accent shifts right, short final stress retracts), stress is not fixed to any position, and stress placement is the primary word-prosodic contrast in every Slovene system — CONFIRMS the catalog's 'lexical' coding (same author as the deciding Greenberg 2006 grammar; peer-reviewed corroboration, does not supersede the grammar's plainer statement). (2) Šekli 2010 (SSJLK 46, open PDF from centerslo.si; Šekli sole author, Smole is the editor) — read: Standard Slovene verb stress is organized into lexical accent paradigms with root vs. infinitive/present-suffix stress and infinitive/present alternations (mériti mérim, nosíti nósim, moríti morím); REFINES the catalog coding with the morphological structure of verb stress. (3) Vermeer 1986 (De Gruyter sandhi volume) — paywalled (30 EUR, no repository copy, no abstract); comparative prosodic-sandhi accentology, unlikely to be the best stress statement; priority low. discovery used Unpaywall/OpenAlex/OpenAIRE/Semantic Scholar APIs and direct fetches.

new_statements.quote: The surface accentual properties of words can be determined by an algorithm applied in the concatenation of individual morphemes, each of which is marked or unmarked for an underlying prosodic feature. [...] (1) Place of stress is assigned to the first rising-pitch morpheme, pitch in the remaining morphemes of these word-forms is ignored; (2) Any remaining falling pitch is shifted one syllable to the right [...]; (4) Short final stress is retracted one syllable, yielding rising pitch on that syllable. [...] In each type, stress placement is ranked above pitch and vowel quantity, which depend on the place of stress.
new_statements.citation: Greenberg, Marc L. 2003. Word prosody in Slovene from a typological perspective. STUF – Sprachtypologie und Universalienforschung 56(3): 234–251. doi:10.1524/stuf.2003.56.3.234 (author copy KU ScholarWorks hdl:1808/5245, via Wayback snapshot 20240421131907)
new_statements.locator: §3 'Lexical assignment of accent', p. 238; §10 Conclusion, p. 247
new_statements.reading: Peer-reviewed, first-hand statement by the same author as the catalog's deciding source: Slovene stress placement is determined by underlying lexical accent marks on morphemes (first rising-accented morpheme gets the stress, with rightward shift of falling accent and retraction of short final stress), not by a phonological edge rule; pitch and quantity are subordinate to the place of stress in every Slovene system (standard and dialects). This is a lexical/morphological accent system = catalog kind 'lexical'. Šekli 2010 (pp. 141–142) independently shows the same for verbs: stress types with root vs. suffix stress and infinitive/present alternations (nosíti ~ nósim).

sources.citation: Šekli, Matej. 2010. Oblikotvorje in jakostni naglas glagola v knjižni slovenščini [Morphology and dynamic stress in the verb in Standard Slovene]. In Vera Smole (ed.), Slovanstvo v slovenskem jeziku, literaturi in kulturi (46. SSJLK), 139–160. Ljubljana: Znanstvena založba FF. (Glottolog credits Šekli & Smole; the PDF names Šekli as sole author, Smole is the volume editor.)
sources.quote: Glagoli z neničto nedoločniško pripono (II–VI), tj. glagoli na -ni-ti, -e-ti/-a-ti, -i-ti, -a-ti, -ov-a-ti/-ev-a-ti, poznajo tri osnovne jakostne naglasne tipe, ki jih je mogoče definirati glede na naglas nedoločnika in sedanjika (naglas na korenu, naglas na nedoločniški/sedanjiški priponi). [...] (a) naglas na korenu v nedoločniku in sedanjiku: mériti mérim [...]; (b) naglas na nedoločniški priponi v nedoločniku in naglas na korenu v sedanjiku [...]: nosíti nósim [...]; (c) naglas na nedoločniški priponi v nedoločniku in naglas na sedanjiški priponi v sedanjiku: moríti morím (pp. 141–142). [Translation: Verbs with a non-zero infinitive suffix (classes II–VI) have three basic dynamic-stress types, definable by the stress of the infinitive and the present (stress on the root, stress on the infinitive/present suffix): (a) root stress in both, mériti mérim; (b) suffix stress in the infinitive, root stress in the present, nosíti nósim; (c) suffix stress in both, moríti morím.]
sources.locator: §1.2 Naglas, pp. 141–142 (and per-class sections B. Naglas, pp. 143–160)
sources.note: Verb stress in Standard Slovene is organized into lexically assigned accent paradigms (naglasni tipi): within a morphological class the stress may sit on the root or on the infinitive/present suffix, and the same verb can shift stress between infinitive and present (nosíti ~ nósim). Class I (zero-suffix) verbs have 'rather heterogeneous stress types', class VII (athematic) verbs 'mostly each their own stress pattern'; the paper says verb stress can be systematised only through a description of a system of stress types — i.e. stress placement is a property of the lexeme/paradigm, not of a phon…

sources.quote: 'Slovenian belongs to the group of languages in which words contain exactly one stressed vowel and in which the position of stress cannot be predicted solely on the basis of the phonological properties of the word or from syllable counting.' Minimal pairs (ígra 'game' vs igrá 'plays'), stress possible on any syllable (Pétra / perésa / gospá), mobile paradigms (móž, možá; góra, goré). sources.quote: 'These stressed syllables are characterized by greater duration as well as by amplitude and pitch prominence. Non-compound words have no more than one stressed syllable. Stress placement is not predictable but is also rarely distinctive in Slovene, although in a few instances different forms of the same noun or verb differ only in stress placement, e.g.: [ˈstʋaːri], [stʋaˈriː], stvari (things, dual vs plural), [ˈnoːsimo], [noˈsiːmo], nosimo.'
